name: Jade Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal day on your factory lines like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run three bagging lines at a frozen vegetable plant. The peas come through a hopper, the machines weigh and seal them, and I change the film rolls and clear jams. The packing hall is four degrees, so I keep a second fleece in my locker even in summer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day comes home with you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The shift pattern, more than the cold. Harvest brings long days, then winter brings shorter weeks, and our mortgage does not follow the pea crop. My partner Dan drives parcels, and we have two children at school; I sometimes use an AI app for a shopping list or homework, but not on the lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the packing crew the big AI promises have fizzled and our baggers still need hands at the film rolls. The winter shift board worries me more than an AI headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can do the job, but last winter a quarter of my wages went missing for three months when the shifts shortened. We have less than a month put aside and very few similar plants nearby. A quiet AI future does not make that mortgage payment easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the three lines and put a fixed slice of every harvest overtime payment into a separate winter account. Dan and I would use our Sunday bill list before we agree to any extra spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the winter pay cut even with AI doing very little. The line work itself feels familiar, which helps me get through a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much did the shorter winter weeks change your bills last time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We used Dan’s Christmas delivery overtime and then the credit card. I hated opening the card statement after the holidays. A small harvest transfer would give us something to use before borrowing again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the plant would you most want to keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the handover between shifts. Our quality checker calls out a weight problem before a whole pallet is wrong, and I trust that more than a bright screen. The work is cold, but the people know their line.

say: I would **tell** the crew the baggers still need operators at the film rolls.
The **winter** shift board matters more to my household than another AI promise.
think: I **know** the job, but a quarter of my winter pay vanished last year.
**Less** than a month of savings leaves our mortgage exposed even in the quiet scenario.
do: **Keep** running the three bagging lines through the next harvest.
**Transfer** a fixed slice of harvest overtime pay into a winter account.
feel: **Anxious** about reduced winter wages, though the familiar line is reassuring.
S0.quote: The winter shift board worries me more than an AI headline.
fieldNote: **Jade** separates a stable machine task from the seasonal pay pattern already straining her household.
She **trusts** the shift handover and plans a wage transfer before relying on Dan’s overtime or credit.

steps.text: Keep operating three bagging lines through the next harvest
Transfer a fixed slice of each harvest overtime payment to winter savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the plant manager for a timetable before anyone promises fewer people on a shift. If an ordering program changes the crop schedule, we need to know which hours move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying and planning could move onto screens first; I would still be clearing jams on the cold line. But if the company merges two lines later, my hours could fall, and Dan’s parcel routes might change too. We cannot carry a mortgage on two shrinking payslips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a paid place on the new line technician course once the equipment and staffing plan are real, and enroll if the place is offered. Until then I would keep the bagging job and cut our streaming bill so the winter account has a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious, not frozen. I have seen a new sealer break every week, so I want the actual line plan before I change course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a paid course place need to cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It needs to happen during paid shifts, not after a twelve-hour harvest day. I cannot lose wages to learn a job the plant might never offer. I would ask whether a technician vacancy is planned before signing up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no paid place or technician vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would stay on the baggers while the hours are there and check advertised machine roles within a bus ride. I would apply only if the posted pay covers our mortgage; there are not many nearby.

say: I would **ask** for a clear timetable for scheduling changes and line staffing.
I would **tell** coworkers the paid technician place must lead to a real role.
think: The **planning** software may arrive first, while my hands are still needed on the baggers.
**Merged** lines could cut my hours just as Dan’s delivery routes are being changed.
do: **Ask** for line-technician training during paid shifts; enrol only if offered and a technician vacancy is planned.
**Cut** streaming costs and keep operating the baggers while staffing is uncertain.
**Check** local machine vacancies if the paid course or technician role is unavailable.
feel: **Anxious** about two possible wage cuts, but able to make a practical plan.
S1.quote: We cannot carry a mortgage on two shrinking payslips.
fieldNote: She **distinguishes** early planning software from later changes to hands-on bagging work.
Her **technician** plan depends on paid shift time and a real vacancy; an unfunded course would risk the wages she needs.

steps.text: Ask for paid-time technician course; enrol only if offered with planned vacancy
Cut the household streaming bill before the winter slowdown
Check advertised machine jobs within a bus ride if no paid technician route appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that the new thinking systems in 2028 do not put robot hands on our film rolls overnight. I would still want proper notice about the machines expected around 2031, and I would ask families to compare bills now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office might use AGI for crop orders in two years, while I keep packing peas until capable robots follow about three years later. I expect our line hours to drop then, and Dan’s parcel work could be squeezed as well. With barely any savings, that would wake me at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month Dan and I would list every mortgage and card payment, stop new card spending, and ask the lender about options before we miss a payment. I would apply for advertised kitchen or care support work within travelling distance only if the posted pay covers our essential bills. Those jobs could change when robots mature too, but they might buy us time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed. I can make a list in daylight, but I would be awake at three doing the same sums again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why look at kitchens or care when robots can reach hands-on work later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am looking for a bridge, not a lifetime guarantee. A school kitchen nearby might need people while a robot packing line is being installed. I would not leave my wage for a vacancy that pays below our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you ask if both incomes fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my mother whether we could stay with her for a short time if the mortgage failed, but I would not assume she has space. I would talk to the lender and Dan first, before frightening the children.

say: I would **tell** the crew to demand notice about robot lines, not confuse 2028 software with 2031 hands-on machines.
I would **urge** families to check their bills while factory wages are still coming in.
think: The **bagging** hours may survive the first AGI wave but fall sharply when capable robots reach the plant.
**Dan’s** parcel income could also shrink, and our savings will not cover a long gap.
do: **List** mortgage and card payments with Dan and stop new card spending this month.
**Ask** lender about options this month before arrears; ask my mother about temporary housing only if mortgage fails, without assuming space.
**Apply** for local kitchen or care vacancies only where posted wages cover essential bills.
feel: **Alarmed** about losing both wages; the sums would keep me awake.
S2.quote: I can make a list in daylight, but I would be awake at three doing the same sums again.
fieldNote: **Jade** gives the hands-on bagging work roughly three years beyond the 2028 thinking AI date.
She **treats** alternative service work as a temporary bridge and makes any application depend on an actual local opening with bill-covering pay.
Her **lender** and family contacts are contingency support if both household wages weaken.

steps.text: List mortgage and credit-card bills and stop new card spending this month
Ask mortgage lender about options this month before any missed payment
Apply to local kitchen or care vacancies only if posted pay covers essential bills
Ask mother about temporary housing only if mortgage fails, without assuming she has space

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my shift that five years gives us time to ask for the actual training budget. The 2031 office systems may redraw orders; the hands-on robot line is more a 2034 problem for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the bagging role will shrink when those capable robots come, and I will be 51 by then. My vocational certificate helped me get this job, but it does not automatically put me in a technician vacancy. Dan and I would still have the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a paid line-maintenance course through work in the first year if the plant offers a place and plans to hire technicians; then I would apply for that posted role. I would move part of each extra harvest wage into savings and keep working my current lines while the course decision is made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious, but five years lets me put each decision on a calendar. I can check the training dates instead of guessing at the lunch table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the plant trains operators but posts no technician job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would finish only the paid course if it is already under way, and look at advertised technician or machine jobs nearby. I would apply only when the pay covers our mortgage and the travel fits school pickup. A certificate by itself is not another wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of harvest pay would you save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start with one overtime shift from each busy pay packet, provided the ordinary bills are covered. Last year we spent the extra as it arrived. I want the winter account to have actual new money in it.

say: I would **ask** the shift about paid training and a posted technician vacancy.
The **robot** replacement of bagging work is a later 2034 question than office AGI in 2031.
think: My **vocational** certificate does not guarantee a technician job at this plant.
With the **mortgage** and few nearby factories, I need paid training and a real wage at the end.
do: **Enroll** in paid line-maintenance training if the plant offers a place and plans a technician vacancy.
**Apply** for its posted technician role after training if pay and school travel work.
**Save** one overtime shift from each busy pay packet when ordinary bills are covered.
feel: **Anxious**, with enough time to put the decisions on a calendar.
S3.quote: A certificate by itself is not another wage.
fieldNote: **Jade** keeps course completion and application to the posted role as separate decisions.
Her **savings** plan uses new harvest overtime wages, while the mortgage and school pickup constrain any later job move.

steps.text: Enroll in paid line-maintenance training if offered with a planned technician vacancy
Apply for the posted technician role after training if pay and school travel work
Transfer one harvest overtime shift per busy pay packet to savings if bills are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade is long enough for the plant to show workers a proper transition plan. I would ask for clear staffing numbers, not a poster about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I would be 53, and by the robot date around 2039 I would be 56. The children would be older, but the mortgage would still need checking against our actual payments. Dan’s routes could change before my bagging line does, so I cannot simply wait ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the bagging work now, take a paid maintenance course if a real place opens in the next few years, and apply for the posted technician job only if the wage covers our bills. In every harvest season I would pay an extra amount off the mortgage when our winter reserve is intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious rather than relieved. A longer runway helps, but two household jobs and one mortgage still sit on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if no maintenance place appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check local vacancies each spring and apply to a posted machine role only when the pay and travel fit. I would not quit the baggers to hope that a course or a vacancy turns up. The nearby list is short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why insist on paid maintenance training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A harvest shift can run long, and I have school pickup to cover with Dan. I need the lessons on paid time so our mortgage payment does not take a hit. Safety practice around live machinery cannot be rushed after work.

say: I would **ask** the plant for actual staffing numbers across the ten-year change.
A **long** runway does not erase Dan’s delivery risk or our mortgage.
think: At 53 in 2036, I **may** still be packing while office work changes.
By the **capable** robot date around 2039, I need a different paid role or a smaller mortgage.
do: **Keep** operating the baggers while vacancies and training places are uncertain.
**Take** paid maintenance training if offered, then apply only to a posted bill-covering technician role.
**Pay** extra off the mortgage from harvest wages when the winter reserve is intact.
feel: **Anxious** about two household wages despite the longer time to prepare.
S4.quote: A longer runway helps, but two household jobs and one mortgage still sit on it.
fieldNote: **Jade** calculates her age at the distinct thinking AI and hands-on robot dates.
She **conditions** training on a paid place and later application on a posted role with sufficient pay.
Her **course** condition reflects long harvest shifts, school pickup and the need for safe practice around machinery.

steps.text: Keep operating the baggers while training places and vacancies are uncertain
Take paid maintenance training if offered with a real place
Apply for a posted technician job after training only if wages cover bills
Pay extra mortgage principal from harvest wages when winter savings are intact

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most because I could lose bagging hours around 2031 before the mortgage is safe, and Dan’s delivery income could shrink too. A wage bridge during paid training and honest notice of robot installation dates would help us plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask factory families what happens to their wages in winter. We already live with short shifts, and a training timetable that ignores those weeks misses the part that hurts.

headlineQuote: We already live with short shifts, and a training timetable that ignores those weeks misses the part that hurts.
portrait: **Jade** Wagner, 43, operates three cold bagging lines at a frozen vegetable factory and holds a vocational certificate.
She **shares** a mortgage and two school-age children with her partner Dan, whose parcel wages also matter to the household.
**Seasonal** hours leave less than one month saved; she tries to transfer harvest overtime before winter shortfalls push them to credit.
She **waits** for proven equipment, paid training and posted local jobs before leaving reliable bagging wages.
**Fast** AGI alarms her because thinking systems arrive in 2028 but capable packing robots may reduce her hours around 2031.
biggestWorry: The 2028 **AGI** picture threatens both Jade’s bagging hours and Dan’s delivery pay once robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** training with a wage bridge, advance robot installation dates, and a real technician vacancy would let her plan.
